title: Switch Transformers, close read: one expert per token and 1.6T parameters
summary: Switch Transformer simplifies MoE's top-k routing down to one expert per token, then adds capacity caps, a simplified load-balancing loss, and a set of training stabilizers. We work through the capacity factor and load-balancing loss by hand, then unpack the speedups over T5, the distillation and multilingual results, and the paradox that more parameters does not mean better downstream performance.
ai_summary: Switch Transformers (Fedus, Zoph, Shazeer, Google, JMLR 2022) simplifies Mixture-of-Experts layers into a switch layer that routes each token to exactly one expert, replacing some of T5's feed-forward networks. The paper uses expert capacity and a capacity factor to handle dynamic routing, a single auxiliary loss to balance load, and proposes selective float32 precision inside the router, smaller initialization, and expert dropout. With the same per-token compute, pre-training is up to 7x faster than T5-Base, and it beats mT5-Base in all 101 languages; Switch-C, with 1.6 trillion parameters, is 4x faster than T5-XXL. Distillation preserves about 30% of the gains, but large models don't always win on reasoning-heavy downstream tasks.
brief: Problem: MoE is complex, communication-heavy, and unstable to train, which has kept it from going mainstream.
Method: send each token to exactly one expert; set an expert capacity; use one load-balancing loss; use selective high precision in the router, smaller initialization, and expert dropout.
Result: with equal compute, pre-training is up to 7x faster than T5-Base; all 101 languages improve; a 1.6-trillion-parameter model is 4x faster than T5-XXL.
Limits: the largest dense-compute variant is still unstable; upstream perplexity gains don't always show up on reasoning downstream tasks; distillation preserves only about 30% of the gain.

paper.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
paper.authors: William Fedus, Barret Zoph, Noam Shazeer

cover.headline: A close read of the Switch paper

nodes.label: The router picks exactly one expert

sections.h: The short version: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In January 2021, Google's William Fedus, Barret Zoph, and Noam Shazeer released this paper; it was published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR) in 2022. Shazeer was first author of the earlier Sparse Mixture-of-Experts paper and second author of T5.

The earlier MoE paper showed that parameter count and computation can be decoupled, but MoE never caught on. This paper argues there are three reasons: **complexity, communication cost, and training instability**. Switch Transformer aims to make MoE simpler and more stable.

The core change is counterintuitively simple: **send each token to exactly one expert**. Until then, people assumed routing to at least two experts was necessary for the gate network to learn to compare and route. This paper finds that k = 1 works, with no quality loss, less computation, and a simpler implementation. It replaces the feed-forward network in every other T5 layer with this "Switch layer" and leaves everything else unchanged.

Around this simplification, the paper provides a recipe for training sparse models well: a simplified load-balancing loss, "selective precision" that uses high precision only inside the router, smaller initialization, and higher dropout inside experts during fine-tuning.

The result: with the same compute, pre-training is up to 7x faster than T5-Base; it beats the multilingual baseline in all 101 languages; and it trained a 1.6-trillion-parameter model that reaches the same perplexity 4x faster than T5-XXL.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: MoE's "pick top-k experts" becomes "pick exactly one", plus capacity caps, a load-balancing loss, and training stabilizers. Parameter count explodes with expert count, while per-token compute stays identical to a dense model.

callout.title: Three concepts worth knowing before you read
callout.text: You don't need deep background; these three are enough:
list: **MoE layer**: many expert networks plus a router; each input is sent to only a few experts. See our close read of Sparse Mixture-of-Experts.
**T5**: Google's encoder-decoder model; it is the baseline for all comparisons in this paper. See our close read of T5.
**FLOPs**: floating-point operations, a measure of compute. "Equal FLOPs" is the premise behind all comparisons in this paper.

sections.h: The Switch layer: each token goes to exactly one expert

blocks.p: First, recall MoE routing. The router computes a score for each expert for a given token, then applies softmax to produce a probability over experts:

parts.desc: Probability that token x goes to expert i
The set of selected experts. Original MoE selects the top k (k ≥ 2); Switch selects only 1—the highest-probability expert.
The expert's output is multiplied by its probability. Even with only one expert, this multiplication gives the router a path for gradients.

formula.note: The paper points out that this exact step—multiplying the output by the gate probability—is why a k = 1 router can still be trained, without needing to compare at least two experts as earlier work feared.

blocks.p: The paper lists three benefits of k = 1:

list: **Less routing computation**: each token is sent to only one expert.
**Expert capacity can be at least halved**: each token takes one slot instead of k.
**Simpler implementation and less communication**: in distributed training, each token only needs to go to one device.

callout.title: Think of it as a hospital with only one appointment
callout.text: The earlier MoE triage desk sent each patient to two or three doctors and then combined their opinions. The Switch triage desk books one appointment with the most suitable doctor. Intuition says you lose some "consultation" benefit, but experiments show almost no loss—and the hospital becomes much simpler and cheaper to run.

sections.h: Capacity: how many tokens each expert can take

blocks.p: TPUs require all tensor shapes to be fixed at compile time, but routing is dynamic: how many tokens in each batch go to each expert isn't known in advance. So every expert needs a fixed **capacity**:

formula.expr: expert capacity = (tokens per batch ÷ number of experts) × capacity factor

parts.sym: Tokens per batch ÷ number of experts
parts.desc: What each expert would receive under perfectly uniform routing.
How much headroom to allow. Above 1, the system can absorb somewhat uneven routing.

formula.note: Tokens above capacity are "dropped": this layer does not process them, and they pass through unchanged via the residual connection. The paper says dropped tokens are usually less than 1%.

fig.title: Worked example: a larger capacity factor drops fewer tokens, but wastes more slots
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: a batch of 12 tokens and 3 experts, with the router sending 6, 4, and 2 tokens to experts 1, 2, and 3. Numbers are ours, computed from Equation (3); this corresponds to Figure 3.
fig.note: A larger capacity factor avoids dropping tokens, but empty slots still consume memory and communication. The paper finds Switch performs better at smaller capacity factors (1.0, 1.25), which matters for memory-constrained large models.

blocks.p: The appendix also tries a "no token left behind" method: overflow tokens go to the second-highest-probability expert instead. It produces no real benefit. The paper speculates that once the model has learned token-to-expert assignments, moving a token to another expert makes things worse.
The earlier MoE used two losses (importance and load). Switch merges them into one, computed for each Switch layer:

parts.desc: The fraction of the T tokens in this batch actually dispatched to expert i. It is counted, so it cannot be differentiated.
The average router probability assigned to expert i across this batch. This can be differentiated.
Number of experts. Multiplying by N keeps the loss at α under uniform routing, regardless of expert count.
Coefficient, set to 10^{−2} throughout: large enough to balance load, small enough not to overwhelm the main cross-entropy loss.

blocks.p: **How does it help?** Gradients can only flow back through P_{i}, and the gradient with respect to P_{i} is proportional to f_{i}. So experts that actually receive more tokens get their router probability pushed down harder, diverting later tokens to other experts.

fig.title: Worked example: the more concentrated the routing, the larger the balancing loss
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: 4 experts, α = 0.01. The f and P numbers are ours, computed from Equations (4)–(6).
fig.note: When unbalanced, expert 1 has f = 0.70, so the gradient on P_{1} is largest and the router is pushed to send fewer tokens to expert 1.

blocks.p: The paper pre-trains on C4 with T5's span-corruption objective (masking 15%). Every model is matched to T5-Base in per-token compute (MoE uses more because it selects two experts), and all models train on the same 32 third-generation TPU cores for the same number of steps. Each MoE and Switch model has 128 experts, with an expert layer in place of every other feed-forward network.

fig.title: Switch vs. MoE and T5: same hardware, who is faster and better
fig.subtitle: From Table 1. Quality is negative log perplexity after 100k steps (closer to 0 is better); "time to target" is hours to reach −1.50.
fig.note: Given the same compute and time, Switch reaches the target fastest. The smaller the capacity factor, the clearer Switch's edge over MoE. Switch-Base+ is scaled up to be as slow as MoE, and it beats all other models on per-step quality.

blocks.p: The paper also records a surprise: lowering MoE's capacity factor from 2.0 to 1.25 made it slower, from 840 to 790. The paper explains that speed depends on both the algorithm and how the underlying implementation is optimized.

sections.h: Three tricks for training sparse models well

blocks.p: **1. Selective precision.** Training in low precision such as bfloat16 saves memory and communication, but the softmax and exponential operations inside the router are precision-sensitive and can make training diverge. Earlier GShard had to run entirely in float32. Switch instead converts the input to float32 only inside the router function, computes, then converts back to bfloat16. Expensive float32 tensors never travel between machines, but you still get float32 stability.

fig.title: High precision only inside the router is enough
fig.subtitle: From Table 2, early in training for a 32-expert model.

blocks.p: **2. Smaller initialization.** Weights are initialized from a truncated normal distribution with standard deviation √(s / n), where n is the input dimension. The paper recommends shrinking the default Transformer scale s = 1.0 by a factor of ten. After 3,500 training steps, average quality improves from −3.60 to −2.72, and the standard deviation across three random seeds drops from 0.68 to 0.01. The same initialization works from 223 million parameters up to more than a trillion.

**3. Expert dropout.** Switch has far more parameters than a dense model with the same compute, so it can overfit on small downstream tasks. Raising dropout everywhere makes things worse; the paper keeps non-expert layers at 0.1 and raises dropout only inside experts to 0.4.

fig.title: During fine-tuning, increase dropout only inside experts
fig.subtitle: From Table 4. d is ordinary dropout, ed is expert dropout.

blocks.p: The appendix also compares several ways to make the router "explore": always choosing the highest score, sampling by probability, applying dropout to the input, and multiplying the input by a random perturbation. In the end it chooses random perturbation (jitter).

sections.h: Scaling: more experts is faster, and even larger dense models can't keep up

blocks.p: **By step:** with per-token compute fixed, expert count doubles from 2 to 256 and parameters grow from 223 million to 14.7 billion, while test loss keeps falling. The 64-expert Switch-Base at step 60k matches T5-Base at step 450k—a 7.5x speedup in steps.

**By time:** Switch adds routing computation and inter-device communication, so step advantages don't automatically become wall-clock advantages. But in fixed time and compute, the 64-expert Switch-Base reaches T5-Base's perplexity in about one-seventh the time.

**Against a larger dense model:** what if that compute were used to train the larger dense T5-Large instead? T5-Large uses 3.5x the per-token compute of Switch-Base, yet Switch-Base is still more sample-efficient and 2.5x faster by wall-clock time.

fig.title: Same compute, dozens of times more parameters
fig.subtitle: From Table 9 (partial). FLOPs/seq is compute per sequence.
fig.note: Switch-C uses only about one-seventh the compute per sequence of T5-XXL, yet has over a hundred times more parameters; the paper says it reaches the same perplexity 4x faster.

blocks.p: The paper pre-trains both T5 and Switch on an improved C4 for 550k steps—about 576 billion tokens—then fine-tunes on a range of tasks.

fig.title: Fine-tuning: better on most tasks, but not always on reasoning
fig.subtitle: From Table 5 (partial), validation sets, higher is better.
fig.note: SuperGLUE improves by 4.4 and 2 points, respectively; knowledge tasks such as closed-book QA improve especially strongly. Only ARC reasoning tasks fail to improve: on the challenge set, Switch-Base underperforms T5-Base, and on the easy set Switch-Large underperforms T5-Large (only the challenge set is shown).

blocks.p: **Distillation:** a trillion-parameter model is hard to deploy, so can a sparse giant be compressed back into a small dense model? The paper finds two tricks useful: initialize the student with the teacher's non-expert weights; and in the loss, mix the teacher's probabilities with the real labels at a 0.25:0.75 ratio. This preserves about 30% of the quality gain.

fig.title: Distilling Switch back to T5-Base size
fig.subtitle: From Table 7. "Retained fraction" is the percentage of the teacher's quality gain over T5-Base that the student keeps.
fig.note: All students are T5-Base models with 223 million parameters; T5-Base itself has quality −1.636. Even compressed to 1% of the original size, the student retains 28% of the teacher's gain.

blocks.p: **Multilingual:** after pre-training for 1 million steps on mC4 in 101 languages, Switch beats the compute-matched mT5-Base in **all** 101 languages, is 5x faster on average, and at least 4x faster in 91% of languages.

sections.h: Trillion-parameter scale: how the three kinds of parallelism fit together

blocks.p: Section 5 of the paper explains how to split the model across thousands of cores. Let the total number of cores be N = n × m, where n is the number of data-parallel replicas and m is the number of model-parallel shards:

list: **Data parallelism**: each core holds a complete copy of the model, processes different data, and synchronizes gradients only at the end of each step.
**Model parallelism**: the large feed-forward matrices are sharded across cores, and every layer performs an all-reduce during both the forward and backward passes.
**Expert parallelism**: each core holds different experts. Routing requires two all-to-all communications: tokens are sent to the core holding their expert, then sent back after the computation.

blocks.p: Switch-C uses only expert parallelism and data parallelism, so it is much smaller than T5-XXL in both width and depth. Switch-XXL has the same compute as T5-XXL, plus the communication overhead of model parallelism. After 250k training steps, both are more than 0.061 better in negative log perplexity than T5-XXL; by comparison, training T5-XXL for another 250k steps improves it by only 0.052.
**But the large models also revealed problems**:

list: **Switch-XXL is occasionally unstable**: the earlier tricks work for Base, Large, and C, but they are not enough for it, so it did not train for the full 1 million steps.

**Better upstream does not mean better downstream**: Switch-C, with 1.6 trillion parameters, scores only 87.7 on SQuAD—lower than the smaller Switch-XXL's 89.6. On SuperGLUE, Switch-XXL, which was pre-trained on only about 503 billion tokens (roughly half of T5-XXL's), scores 87.5, below T5-XXL's 89.3; but on knowledge tasks such as closed-book QA, it surpasses the previous best result. The paper's summary: Switch's upstream gains transfer more readily to knowledge tasks, and less fully to reasoning tasks.

callout.title: “The more parameters, the smarter the model”
callout.text: This paper is itself a counterexample. Switch-C has roughly four times as many parameters as Switch-XXL, but Switch-XXL does far more computation per token and still performs better on downstream tasks like SQuAD. The paper's explanation is that the relationship among fine-tuning quality, per-token compute, and total parameter count is "not yet understood." Roughly speaking, having more parameters is like "knowing more," and doing more compute is like "thinking more deeply"—the two cannot substitute for each other.

list: **The order is reversed in one sentence**: Section 3.1 says the 64-expert model "reached T5-Base's step-60k level at step 450k." Given the 7.5x speedup, it should be the other way around: Switch reaches T5-Base's step-450k level by step 60k.
**"About 10x" is really about 7x**: Sections 5.6 and 8 both say Switch-XXL uses about 10x the per-token compute of Switch-C. According to Table 9, 6.3 trillion ÷ 890 billion is about 7x.

**"100x parameters" is really about 17x**: Table 6's note says a sparse model with "100x more parameters" can be distilled back to a small model, but the teacher Switch-Base in the table has 3.8 billion parameters and the student has 223 million—about 17x. The main text's "about one-twentieth of the parameters" is closer.
**Attention head counts don't match**: Table 1 says Switch-Base+ increases attention heads "from 14 to 16," but in Table 9 both T5-Base and Switch-Base have 12 heads.
**"Lower is better" is backward**: the note for Appendix Table 11 says negative log perplexity is "lower is better," but everywhere else in the paper it is higher is better (closer to 0 is better).

**Is the perturbation added or multiplied?** The appendix says a "multiplicative" perturbation is applied to the input, but the appendix pseudo-code **adds** a random number near 1 to the routing scores.

sections.h: Since then: MoE has become a mainstream choice for large models

list: **The Top-1 vs. Top-2 debate**: Switch proved that routing to a single expert works; many later open-source MoE models went back to two or more experts per token, plus finer-grained expert partitioning. The right number is a trade-off among quality, communication, and hardware.
**Load balancing is still the core problem**: Switch's auxiliary loss (α · N · Σ f P) became a common practice. The last article in this series, DeepSeek-V3, will look at a different approach.
**The stabilization tricks have been widely adopted**: high precision in the router, smaller initialization, and similar lessons later became common in large-model training.
**"Better upstream does not mean better downstream"**: this phenomenon is a reminder that pre-training perplexity alone is not enough to evaluate sparse models.

blocks.p: This series now changes direction, from "adding parameters" back to the Transformer's own components. The next article is on **rotary position embeddings (RoPE)**, which nearly all of today's open-source large models use to tell the model where each token is in the sequence.

sections.h: Check yourself: have you really understood it?

quiz.q: When tokens are sent to only one expert, why can the router still be trained?
options: Because the expert output is multiplied by the routing probability p_{i}(x), so gradients can flow back to the router through this multiplication.
Because the router is fixed and doesn't need training.
quiz.why: Earlier work assumed that at least two experts had to be compared for routing to be learned. The paper points out that as long as the output is multiplied by the gate probability, the router receives a gradient, so k = 1 can learn too.

quiz.q: What is the cost of setting the capacity factor too high?
options: More empty slots, wasting memory and compute, and increasing communication.
quiz.why: A large capacity factor drops fewer tokens, but each expert has to allocate slots according to capacity, and unused slots are wasted. The paper finds Switch performs best at small capacity factors between 1.0 and 1.25.

quiz.q: Switch-C has 1.6 trillion parameters, so why does it underperform the 395B-parameter Switch-XXL on SQuAD?
options: Switch-XXL uses far more compute per token; the paper says the relationship among fine-tuning quality, compute, and parameter count is not yet understood, and more parameters cannot fully replace more computation.
quiz.why: Section 8 of the paper discusses this "anomaly" specifically. It shows sparse models' advantages are clearer on knowledge tasks, while reasoning tasks may still need more compute.

blocks.p: After reading this article, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What is the difference between a Switch layer and the original MoE layer? What are the benefits of k = 1?
What are expert capacity and the capacity factor? What happens to dropped tokens?
How is Switch's load-balancing loss calculated? How does it encourage balance?
What problems do selective precision, smaller initialization, and expert dropout each solve?
Compared with T5-Base and T5-Large, where does Switch's speed advantage come from?
How much quality can distillation preserve?
Why do we say "better upstream does not mean better downstream"?

main.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity (arXiv:2101.03961 v3)

sources.note: This article is based on version 3 of the paper on arXiv (the content of the official JMLR 2022 version); the first version was released in January 2021. Tables marked "Illustrative" use numbers we chose and are computed from the paper's formulas. The "about 7x" and "about 17x" figures are our calculations based on the paper's tables. The practices of later open-source MoE models come from public sources and are not in this paper.
